SET CONTRACT (the engine depends on every line of it)
FORMAT

- Three top-level groups in this order: <g id="far">, <g id="mid">, <g id="near">. Inside them, one named group per
  object (lowercase snake_case: table, chair_3, wall_screen, window_2). Draw the walls and the floor complete behind
  the furniture, so nothing has a hole when the layers slide apart.
- Light and surface effects go in classed groups inside each depth group: class="lm-shadow" (cast and contact
  shadows), class="lm-light" (light patches), class="lm-atmos" (haze, light shafts), class="lm-texture" (texture
  marks), class="lm-outline" (strokes, only if the style uses outlines), class="lm-hi" (highlight edges),
  class="lm-glow" (glow, only if the style uses it). Base shapes stay outside these groups.
- No <text>, no letters or numbers anywhere, no <image>, no filters, no masks, no clip paths, no external references.
  Gradients only where the style block allows them: two stops, palette colours only.
- Up to 700 KB per file; coordinates as integers or one decimal.
- Every position in the brief below (percent of height, thirds, left and right) refers to the visible 1920 x 1080

- A mid or near object cropped by a frame edge continues at least 120 px into the overscan, so a camera move never
  shows its cut edge.

LIGHTS AND LIT THINGS (which palette tones draw them)

- Small lights (an exit sign, an LED, a card reader, a lift indicator): plant hi for green, accent hi for red, with
  lm-glow around them only if the style uses glow.
- A lamp's or a screen's spill on nearby surfaces: light at 0.3 to 0.6 fill-opacity in lm-light (a cool screen spill:
  glass base at 0.1 to 0.2).
- Night window glass: sky deep, with shadow over it at about 0.6 fill-opacity in lm-shadow; distant city lights as
  small light-coloured dots.
- A light or shadow shape lies only on the surface it lands on. Where an object of the same layer stands on that
  surface (a chair on a sunlit floor, a cup in a pane pattern on a table), the shape stops at the object's outline and
  never paints across it; light that falls on the object itself is drawn on the object's own shapes. A shadow or light
  shape laid over a chair makes the chair look like glass (the office sets of 2026-10-12).

STYLE: GLOW-FLAT (for science, technology and big-idea explainers; places after dark lit by screens and lamps)
- Bright, simplified geometric shapes on a dark ground; perspective simplified but correct; shapes have designed asymmetry, not template roundness.
- No outlines. Flat fills with a rim of light (lm-hi) on the edges that face a light source.
- Light sources are the subject: screens, lamps, windows of the city. Glow in lm-glow only, around light sources and on the surfaces they hit (concentric shapes stepping down in opacity 0.35, 0.2, 0.1, or a two-stop radial gradient).
- Few, large shapes; details only where the light falls.
- The emitter is the focal point; lit and reflective surfaces (a desk top, glass, a polished floor) become secondary sources; light falls off radially, and detail and clarity drop away from the light. Design the darks on purpose: night is not a darker daytime picture.
- Light: Night: the room is lit by its sources. Each source throws a pool of its colour on the nearest surfaces; everything else falls into the dark wall and floor tones.
- Texture: None, or a few faint star-like specks of light in a window view.
- Depth: Far: darker and bluer; the city through windows as flat lit window grids. Near: the darkest silhouettes against the glow.

A residential building site on a former car park at the edge of a town centre in a temperate country, about eighteen months into a two-year build: a five-storey block of 36 flats with a reinforced-concrete frame, its red-brown brick outer walls rising behind a galvanised tube-and-fitting scaffold. About 60 people on a busy day (the main contractor's team and the trades). The plot, about 70 m by 45 m, sits inside a 2.4 m plywood hoarding along the street; at the entrance a vehicle gate and a separate pedestrian gate with a turnstile; beside them a two-storey stack of steel cabins (site office and induction room, canteen, drying room, toilets); between the cabins and the building a yard of crushed stone with fenced pedestrian routes, a materials area and new drainage trenches being dug across it.
Architecture:

- the ground: compacted grey crushed stone with tyre ruts and shallow puddles; the site road edged by mesh fence panels; pedestrian routes fenced off from the plant with mesh fence panels on concrete-filled feet and marked with signs
- safety points where they really are: a site rules board of blue mandatory signs at the pedestrian gate, a fire point by the cabins (extinguishers on a stand, a red fire sign, a site alarm call point), a green first-aid sign on the canteen cabin, a green assembly-point sign on the hoarding near the gate

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- neon on everything
- glow on surfaces with no light source
- outlines
- a muddy dark with no clear light shapes
- night drawn as a darker copy of the day scene
Not in this world:
- a generic site with no character, or a chaotic, unsafe one (the site is well run; the lessons are about people's choices in it)
- real brands, logos, words or numbers on boards, signs, cabins, plant or tags
- people in the sets (the cast is separate); plant (excavators, dumpers, telehandlers) only parked and at rest, or as separate props
- a tower crane (lifting on this site is done by a telehandler and, on lift days, a mobile crane)
- an open edge, a trench or a scaffold lift without its guardrails, or a ladder not tied at the top
- safety signs with words; every sign is a pictogram in its ISO 7010 shape and colour
- anything stored on a pedestrian route, in front of the fire point or on the scaffold's ladder landings
